doc.title: Johnny Varro interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001

title: Writing charts and the Stompy Jones premiere
summary: How he writes and copies parts, and tomorrow's Swing 7 set.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Beautiful stuff. Do you sit at a piano when you write?

I might try some harmonies. You know if you write for four horns you might want to get the best harmony and open it up a little bit. I’ll do that and some passing tones, to make sure that it jives. A lot of it I do from my head originally and then I’ll try it at the piano and make some changes as I go along. But the idea comes from up here.
Do you write all your own parts out and all that?

I write, yeah, yeah. I’m a stickler for neatness. And I’ve been handed so much music that has been scribbled. And they say, “Here, play this” and you’ve got to — if you can’t interpret the music you’re not going to be able to play it. So I make sure that I write it clear enough that it’s legible and understandable. And then if it’s not played correctly it’s their fault.
You don’t want to give them any excuses.
No. In fact, later on tomorrow I think we have a set with the Swing 7 at five o’clock.
Oh great. I’m glad you told me that.
Yeah. And I’ve got a lot of new stuff there that’s on the new CD.

And we’re not going to rehearse, I’m just going to throw it at them. In fact I finished a chart yesterday afternoon was it? No yesterday morning before I came here. I finished it out, I copied it and we’re going to play it. It’s never been played before. An Ellington tune.
Yeah. Duke Ellington, “Stompy Jones.” A great old piece.
